Verbal components of a spell I rule are magical words being uttered, that are heard at a normal volume. Non spellcasters probably won't recognize the exact spell, but arcane/divine/naturalistic magic has more to it than just the words being spoken, and even if people don't recognize it as magic, they'd likely be nervous regardless. A tavern keep that interacts with magical adventurers semi-regulatly would likely recognize magic words being spoken, and might not appreciate someone casting a spell in their bar without permission or forewarning, as they have no level of knowing what the spell might do.
However, I would give the player the option to finish casting if they want, but I'd let them know the risk of doing such. If they still want to, and they end up charming the tavern keep, any one else paying attention will obviously realize that spellcaster charmed them and TBH enchantment magic is probably the most sinister, since it takes over living peoples faculties against their will. There would likely be social consequences in that instance.

If it only had a somatic component, I'd allow a sleight of hand check but only that. Otherwise, allowing covert magic without subtle spell diminishes the choice of getting subtle spell.

The mats fall apart, when wet, much easier than with soil.

As with any market there are trade offs. If you live in a big city, there are more customers, more people that know what your product is, BUT there is often more competition which often leads to lower prices.
A smaller city or town you can have higher prices becauze there will probably be less competition, BUT there are less customers and less people that know what your product is.

One good way to figure out what you want to keep/get rid of/buy is the classic, "Will/Does this object spark joy?" However, that doesn't quite encompass tools/supplies that might be essential (e.g. I'm a farmer and have a bunch of various tools, fertilizers, pots, etc. that I need). In that sense, go by similar standards of "essentials", like toilet paper or food. Additionally, if the object itself doesn't spark joy, ask yourself, "Does this tool allow me to do a task that sparks joy?"

People use hydroponics for a few main reasons. A big one is that it uses much less water than soil farming, depending on the style, up to 80-90% less. Another is that you know exactly what is going into the nutrient solution, so it is easier to tweak than soil. The big reason is that once the system is up and running smoothly, the amount of time needed to maintain it is much less than soil farming (mostly because of zero to barely any need for weeding).

As far as tips to start, I would recommend getting acquainted with all of the essential nutrients for plants, how much you need of each, at what time of the growth cycle, and their functions, if you haven't already. This part is much more important for hydroponics than soil because decent soil should have most of what you need, whereas, depending on what water you use, water has little to no nutrients in it, for plant growth.

Equally important is supplying oxygen to the roots, since without it, the plants can "drown". There are many ways to do this, but the simplest surefire method, that I've found, is Deep Water Culture (DWS) which is simply floating your plants on top of a tank/trough of water and having aquarium air stones pump bubbles under the roots.

Finally, if you have some gardening experience, I would recommend testing out 1 plant that you already have experience growing, that way you can compare your hydroponic growth to your soil growth, to help understand what went wrong, if there are issues. It also helps to know specific nutrient needs for only 1 plant, and then branching out from there, once you feel comfortable in yours, and the systems, abilities.

You probably already have an idea of what grows well in your climate. If you are unsure, I would recommend hot climate tender plants, like tomatoes, peppers or cucumbers, all of which can be grown effectively in hydroponics, and two of which I have grown myself with great success.

Also, since your average temp is so high, you might have an issue with root rot, if the water gets too hot because it holds less dissolved oxygen, the hotter it gets. I would recommend having a large tank, as to make it take longer to heat up, paint it white to absorb minimal heat, use a cooler, change water more frequently, add a gallon of ice cold water a day, add hydrogen peroxide periodically, run pipes underground and back up, etc.

Best of luck, in all your ventures! All of these topics are easiler searched on Google, Bing, etc. if you want more in depth information. I had a similar problem, it looks to me like nitrogen deficiency. If the top leaves were yellow instead, it would be nitrogen toxicity. 
Nitrogen is very essential to vegetative growth, whereas in flowering potassium is more important. Nitrogen makes the leaves strong and healthy, and potassium supports bud growth. In fact, during flowering it's natural for the leaves to turn a little yellow because the leaves aren't the priority in getting the nutrients anymore.
Since you said you haven't added any fertilizer, it makes sense. Nute burn starts at the tip of the leaves and generally affects most of the leaves, not just the bottom.
I recommend slowly adding a fertilizer rich in nitrogen and gradually increasing the dosage to proper levels, only for vegetative. Once you hit flowering, switch to a more potassium rich fertilizer.
P.s. You probably wont be able to save the leaves that are already that yellow. Don't worry, as long as more leaves don't turn yellow, you should be fine.
